review_text_raw:
I'd personally like it more if I didn't do hacking for a living.

I can't help but find flaws in its guitar-hero style approach to cyber security.

This game is at its strongest when it closest resembles real hacking: problem solving through enumeration, weaponization and exploitation. This is especially evident when you are plundering compromised hard drives and linking information together to achieve a goal.

The game is at its weakest when it relies too much on the "hacking tools". It's like a less comprehensive version of Metasploit and Nmap where you just use the same modules over and over again. For me, it got boring fast and I would constantly try to rush through the repetition.

Props to whole game being playable from the CLI though.

Solid game, but if you want to do real hacking, go to TryHackMe or HackTheBox.

8/10

EDIT: I have had a couple people contact me, thank you for doing so. I didn't mean to sound cynical, the developer took on a huge challenge and he largely succeeded. Development is really tough.

He got pretty much everything right about the industry however. And there is a balance between real hacking and accessibility being juggled here. When I say, it's the "guitar hero" of hacking, I mean that while the hacks being pulled off are completely plausible in real life, the execution is much, much harder.

It's a video game, so I should have allowed it more grace. If you have a passing interest in hacking, I'd absolutely recommend this game. If you want to do the real deal, feel free to contact me and we can set up some CTFs.

Oh and one more thing: the game's soundtrack is super fun to listen to while doing the real thing. (:

Revised score: 9/10

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1]What is happening in the game:[/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
    [*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
    [*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
    [*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
    [*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
    [*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
    [*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
    [*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
    [*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
    [*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
    [*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
    [*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
    [*]This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.
[/list]

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

Greetings,
BirdCute

review_text_raw:
Coming from someone with experience in ethical hacking, wireless security, networking, firewalls, server administration and so on, this game covers: 
- basic linux commands
- the most basic understanding of nmap (as in just the command that probes an IP lol)
- Repetitive Exploits in the form of exe files that require a port number
- Data enumeration
- Adding a Shell to a node in order to overload proxy's

Pros:
- GUI is cool to look at
- Simplifies hacking for a somewhat better understanding
- Some parts require you to actually use your brain

Cons:
- Only has a handful of linux commands
- Repetitive
- Not an accurate representation of the cyber kill chain process
- I had to create a "Settings" file with a bunch of random settings that I had to get online for the game to actually display on the screen

But the game is pretty cool.

review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

++ Pros
- Command Line
- Simple Gameplay
- Uses Real Ports (SSH 22, Web Server 80, ect)
- Immersive Gameplay
- Excellent Soundtrack
- Tons of Easter Eggs

-- Cons
- Short Storyline
- Repetitive
- Occasional Bugs

To be frank, I've taken this game and played it for at least three times the amount of time steam has recorded me on it. And in all honesty, this game has tons of charm. Yes, the storyline is short, however the immensely fitting soundtrack and numerous textual gems in the game assists in making this game amazing. There will be points in this game where you will laugh at a silly request or character, or even a small piece of dialogue, and there will be points in which you will need to set the game down for an hour or so to contemplate the actions you've decided to take, or the gravity of the mistake you've potentially made. The atmosphere generated by the soundtrack is immensely fitting for the gameplay, and (in my personal opinion) does make you feel rather devious as you weave through the security measures on a character's computer to further the game. And when your "computer" crashes for the first time, expect to freak out for a second. It is just a game, but some of the featues that make the game such an excellent hacking sim can, and will, startle you. :P

With the upcoming additions and DLC, including multiplayer and new storylines, I wouldn't hesitate to pick this game up again and start playing.

TL;DR - 10/10, l33t haxx0r would reccomend.

review_text_raw:
While this game is being sold as a "hacking simulator", a debate will likely rage about what exactly it simulates. In either case, it comes suspiciously close to being a realistic simulation of hacking. So close, in fact, I'm left wondering why the dev didn't go the extra yards to make it inarguably so (maybe something he can shoot for in the future). Realism nit-picking aside, this game is full of very realistic nods to hacker and IRC culture, and in broad strokes, represents some of what goes on in actual exploits. While the experience of compromising systems is streamlined for the sake of keeping it an actual game (again, is it a puzzle game or a simulator?), in that "push a button, get bacon" sort of way you see in "hacker" movies, there was still much in the game that reminded me of taking the OSCP (for those who know my pain, you will find much in each mission to make you smile in that corpse-like rictus you had while laughing at emails and files during enumeration pratice in the Offsec lab).

After a while, I realized I was playing not so much because of the faux-hacking experience, but because there was a rather compelling story unfolding. Can't pick that apart without spoiling it, so I'll critique the gameplay instead (positives first):

[b]Pros:[/b]
This game is hilarious in a sick, twisted way. References to chan and IRC culture litter the storyline. While the majority of gameplay involves limited exploit combinations, there are moments where you don't know what the f**k is going on, and you have to think fast to avert a crisis. If you're into security culture, you'll find your intuition meshes well with the challenges, and you can improv what to do most of the time. It's like a Drunk History version of real hacking, so it's probably an ideal game to play while you're drunk.

People with zero knowledge of hacker culture or basic unix commands and quad notation will walk away familiar with all of the above.

The game is cheap, so whether you enjoy the simplistic, repetitive nature of the "hacking" it simulates, you won't regret the purchase, because it will entertain you regardless. The story itself is worth the price, and the way the story is told using the genre is clever.

If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys.

[i]Maybe the two of you should consider a collab or something...[/i]

[b]Cons:[/b]

Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu. 

[b]Also, why write so many missions for lelzsec, but make it so easy to permanently lose your chance to access them -- it was like a quarter of the game just gets skipped automagically because there isn't a clear choice presented to the player that an alternate path exists![/b]

Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer.

To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k).

Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off.

[b]OVERALL[/b]:
Short game. In 20 hours you can play through twice and get all the achievements, and you compulsively will, despite the bugs that might force you to start a new game because something is glitched and can't recover [though the developer is working hard to patch all these, props to him]. There are enough Easter Eggs and humorous logs to make you anxious that you missed some the first time. More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved. 

For $8-ish, I felt like I got more than I paid for and told my friends to play it for the lulz.

review_text_raw:
Fun simulator and manual dexterity game with puzzle elements. You do not have to be a computer-whiz to enjoy Hacknet, but people comfortable at the command-line will enjoy it more. This game takes elements of computer system and makes a fun game out of them. For example, you don't have to know what program runs on the internet port 25, you just have to type that number at the end of the command.

The game simplifies the technical things and makes it fun, while leaving enough to make it also a challenge. It does a great job with the user interface, and I found everything very intuitive. I kept thinking of another hacking simulator, Uplink, and I think Hacknet does a better job with the game interface.

The gameplay was hit and miss for me. I felt like the game is not always consistent with the in-game logic. Find out a password, later it has changed. The commands are not always consistent (like "../filename" does not always work). Some commands are logged on servers but not others, and the purpose of server logs is not made clear. All these are minor issues, because the game is obviously going for fun not realism, but I wish the game did a better job informing me how the game world worked.

Hacknet is best when it feels like an open world, where every bit of information gathered could lead to a new story, when it is used in the right way. Unfortunately, most of the Hacknet stories are trails of breadcrumbs that lead from the email message to a server file, back to a workstation command, and finally a reply message of completion. And these stories can start to feel pretty repetitive, since most of the story time is spent hacking the server defenses, using the same weapon arsenal, each time.

All that said, the stories are well-written, even though most are short, including the primary Bit narrative. The game uses text assets to populate the game world to good effect. And there were just a few opportunities to figure things out independently, which made me feel pretty clever. All said and done, I would recommend this game, especially to computer enthusiasts, with the warning that you will be typing, with some easy timed typing challenges.

I enjoyed Hacknet on an ubuntu linux gaming desktop, with radeon mesa graphic drivers.

review_text_raw:
[b][i]Hacknet[/i] is an absolutely outstanding hacker-simulator experience.[/b] They really got it right. For what may look like a monotonous and boring text-based experience, this game will get your heart pounding and leave you on the edge of your seat. 

[b]The experience makes you really [i]feel[/i] like a hacker.[/b]

[i]Essentially, this is a sandbox computer world simulator not that different from our own, where you will enter commands and slink around the internet completing quests.[/i] Commands in many cases are nearly identical to IRL commands (particularly thinking of DOS, here). The UI is perfect - especially QoL upgrades like autocomplete, and a great help function really go a long way here. The story and music are awesome, too.

[b]Pros:[/b]
+Excellent hacker experience
+Sandbox-type world where you really feel like you have open-ended control
+Metric tons to do
+You can play this at work and nobody will know any better
+Excellent music
+Outstanding story
+Simple UI, especially if you are used to command-based OS

[b]Cons:[/b]
-Not really any that I can think of; I've even had people that are not computer nerds at all try this and they get hooked just as quickly as I did

[b]Totally worth the experience.[/b] This game really thinks outside the box, and makes you rethink your ideas on what makes a game fun.

review_text_raw:
Steam needs to update the rating system. This thumbs up/down is just too simplistic. While I do recommend the game for those who never played a hack "sim" before, I get the feeling that some people who are used to Uplink will be disappointed.

Uplink is the only game like this one I've played, and Hacknet is obviously inspired by it, so this is basically a comparison between the 2.

If you played Uplink this will be a walk in the park. Aside from visuals, there's nothing here that Uplink didn't do better back in 2001. With the excepton of a couple of moments, all missions are exactly the same all the way through, so it gets repetitive quite fast. 

There's no sense of danger or urgency Uplink gives you. Nobody will come after you, there's no police, companies you hack won't give a shit. Despite of what the game tells you right at the beggining, there's no need to cover your tracks. In Uplink, everytime you hack into a system it's a race against time. In Hacknet there's nothing like it. Once you block a trace you can spend as much time as you want in any system.

There's no rig upgrades, no rewards, nothing like it. You just complete the mission, get a "thank you" email and move on to the next.  

Both games have a story, but Uplink is more of a sandbox. After you get the hang of it you can do whatever you want and follow the story whenever you want. Hacknet, on the other hand, is pretty linear. That's a big dissapointment, specially after a great "wtf do I do now" moment right in the beggining. After that, you get the feeling you're never safe, but unfortunately nothing like that ever happens again. Storywise, Uplink is way more interesting, while Hacknet is cliche and way too simplistic.

That's the main problem with this game. It's way too easy. Uplink is infuriating unforgiven to the player. Once you start to mess with big companies, one small screw up means game over. Add that to the fact that the game is pretty much a roguelike, so it's not like you can go back to a previous save, you have to start all over again. In Hacknet, you don't need to worry about that. Like I said before, there's no need to clean after you. If you get caught, all you need to do is change your ip adress.

Anyway, if you never played a hacking "sim" before, this might be a good place to start. Like Uplink, It's really easy to get into, you don't need to now anything about code to play both games, and they give you a good sense of immersion.   

Hacknet has a good concept, but is way too simple for those looking for a challenge. I hope the "Labyrinths" expansion adds more substance to the game.

5/10

Real hacking is very complex and tedious so making a game out of it is certainly something that requires imagination and creativity, and the fact that Hacknet gives you an immersive sense of intelligence and power really makes me believe they've accomplished that balance.

Definitely recommend.

Note: Game length averaged me about 11-12 hours.

An absolutely engaging and wonderful game. This is one of those gems that lingers in your library for a while ominously taunting you. I'm going to break this review up in a few sections. The game lets you explore what it's like to be a hacker. Well more of a stereotypical movie meme hacker, but still that's a perk here. You should expect to be snooping into people's computers, reading their emails, and finding all of their dirty secrets. With that in mind this game plays more like an information-gathering puzzle simulator.

1. Gameplay
This may be the biggest "fear" new players may have after viewing the trailer. This game involves typing out commands in a terminal, but really it's just similar to a "text based" adventure with commands. If you're new to using a CMD line (terminal) this is a perfect engaging way to become more familiar with how it works. Just like any new game once you get familiar with the controls you'll breeze through it. There is a clean graphic user interface that makes navigating the game environment (with your mouse) very intuitive. You are taught how to play in a standard tutorial so you're not just thrown out into the ocean expecting to be a 1337 h@ck0r. You will encounter several high and low points that will continue to test what you've learned. At no point in the game did I feel like it was repetitive. You will have time to become familiar with your tools and soon after your tools will grow, allowing you to tackle harder and more complex hacker challenges. 

2. Story
No spoilers. I can say that there is a story and that you will be highly involved with in. There is a lot of mysteries, and plenty of interesting characters to learn about. I should mention that each new play through of the game will have many events randomized. In addition the story continues in the DLC and that I found it totally worth it.

3. Graphics
I find the graphics to be a nice blend between modern techno sci-fi and retro website design. It's actually quite an interesting blend of styles that seems to work out well. I can safely say this [b]isn't[/b] just a game where you look into singular black box and type commands. 

4. Final Thoughts
It's good. I personally had some doubts but once I started playing I couldn't stop. I wouldn't be leaving a review if I didn't think it deserved more attention.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.


[h1] RATING: 8.5/10 [/h1]

This game drew me in when I was younger in the Linux world and I soon found that it was reinforcing (sort of) my basic skills that I was learning at that time. The OUTSTANDING soundtrack helped to draw me in and soon I was hooked. I am in the education field, and when I found this game, I was teaching some students basic command line stuff on their Chromebooks with overthewire.com/wargames/bandit and a terminal emulator in their Chrome browsers. 

This is a fun game that helps reinforces the basics while making you feel like you are in a murder mystery and trying to save the good guys and their kin. The soundtrack ALONE is well work the under $5 you will pay for this game. Massive Kudos to the hours of fun I have had over and over, replay after replay.

review_text_raw:
In [i]Hacknet[/i], you play as a computer user who has just been bestowed a unique operating system (OS) with tools that can hack different computers. As the game progresses, you will discover new hacking tools, join other factions of hackers, fulfill hacking job contracts to build your reputation, and solve the game’s central mystery.

What I love about [i]Hacknet[/i] is the high level of immersion and engaging pacing. With my headphones on, listening to the adrenaline-pumping soundtrack, I voraciously took on one hacking contract after another. Before long, two to three hours have flown by. The game's missions, though all require hacking, vary in objects and pacing. Because of that, I did not find gameplay repetitive, and I used every opportunity to familiarize myself with the tools I had at my disposal. All of this prepared me for the climatic final mission, which totally did not disappoint.

[i]Hacknet[/i] is novice-friendly, but some players may find it having a slightly steep learning curve. Players will be at an advantage if they can type fast, has used *nix (e.g. Linux) shell commands, and/or are familiar with text-based OSes. This is because the user interface of [i]Hacknet[/i] is austere, with typing as your primary form of input. Still, there are simple graphics to depict hacking progress, network of computers, and directory trees. You can use your mouse from time to time as means of in-game navigation as I did.

[i]Hacknet[/i]'s appeal aside from immersion and pacing is really its simplicity. The players will always be given all the tools they would need to complete missions. So, the real challenge is to figure out which tool(s) to use to hack the computers and phones, and to do it quickly and efficiently. So, think fast! Type fast and furious! Once the dust has settled, snooping around the hacked machines and reaping your rewards are gratifying.

At the time of this review, [i]Hacknet[/i] is my favourite hacking-themed game. It’s fast, it’s empowering, and it’s extremely gratifying -- especially after a challenging mission. I highly recommend this game to those who wish an adrenaline-pumping, brain-teasing, text-based adventure game.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a great intro to Unix command line interface.  There are lots of basic command line tutorials out there but to build muscle memory, you need to use commands like cd (change directory) and ls (list content) over a 100 times.  However who wants to change directory and list directory content over 100 times?  Thus most tutorials will let you practice a command couple times then move on--not building muscle memory.  Hacknet is the solution! In Hacknet you will connect to multiple computers on the net, traversing the file system via the command line and it before you know it you will build muscle memory.  The story is well written and compelling enough that typing the same commands over and over (grinding) to "flip the page" of the story is worth it.

If you are doing this for just the learning purposes--many realistic hacking game reviews recommend Hacknet as a prerequisite.  I recommend getting the Labyrinth expansion because it add new tools to learn.  When no new tools or commands are offered, start the Labyrinth expansion mission, The Kaguya Trials--start Labyrinth missions early rather than later.  Hacknet stops introducing new concepts about mid way and the Labyrinth expansion brings the learning back.   Mid Labyrinth missions, decide when you practiced enough and stop playing.

review_text_raw:
***This only takes the base game into account***

Ever wanted to crack down on some real terminal action to get a peek at what this hacking business is all about? Wonder no more, as Hacknet is here to "teach" you what "hacking" is. 

Immersive, intelligent and just enough unix-commands at your disposal, Hacknet will convince anyone not computer savvy or not paying close enough attention that the things on your monitor sure looks like something you shouldn't be doing, almost like dark wizardry magic. For the most part, the game offers up this illusion at an convincing rate while being beginner-friendly. However, in the world of hacking, there is very little hand holding, so the faster you understand what the ropes are, the better.

To deliver a convincing hacking experience, music is paramount - as Uplink back in the day taught everyone. Here is really delivers, with everything from ambient barrens tunes fit for the breaks between each mission, to serious business from The Algorithm and wildly intense adrenaline pumping Carpenter Brut songs. Hats off, this album is even worth listening to way after you've finished the game. 

As for the the main story, while not top shelf, is interesting enough to keep searching around for clues and getting a better grasp at what's going. As with any self respecting game that depicts hacking, it should have its sheer selectino of surprise elements, and Hacknet doesn't disappoint. However, this is usually found in side missions. The main story should've done more of that as well.

For each time you play, the game changes up names, IPs etc for the nodes to try to keep things sort of fresh, but the missions are mostly the same. All in all, Hacknet is a very solid, albeit simple at times, attempt at creating an immersive, "real enough" hacking simulator that most importantly is -FUN-. The list of unix commands are however at times frustratingly limited, especially if you know what you're doing. Since most of the game is very well laid out in terms of the interface, you start taking it for granted that you should be able to do more than you actually are allowed to. 

For example, "rm file*" will not work since the terminal doesn't support wildcards. Pathing is also needlessly tedious, as it doesn't properly understand using root-nodes in paths. Props however for making it possible to furk up yourself, which is how it should be. Paying attention and going "outside the beaten path" is usually rewarded.
 
Hacknet requires reading and understanding of its core concepts to get the most out of the experience. For those persistent enough, the game also delivers some hilarious content as a nod to the efforts. Here's to hoping the developer makes more content to this game, as the main game is rather short. It'll take you only around 5-6 hours for the main campaign. A multiplayer mode would've been awesome in addition to random missions. 

Rating: 8/10 - Play it!

This is a game I never thought I'd fall in love with. 
This is a game I never thought I'd spend so much time on.
This is a game I never thought I'd be so invested in.
This is a game I never thought would be a long time favorite.

I could go on about how much I adore this game, but the fact of the matter is that you're looking at the reviews to gauge whether or not this is worth the buy. Am I wrong? Most likely not.

This is a game where you can feel like the badass hacker you've always wanted to be. Don't you dare lie to yourself and say that you've never wanted to be that shady figure in those movies or be like Sombra and hack the world. I promise you this game can fulfill that fantasy, and so much more.

In terms of gameplay, yes, it does get a bit repetitive, but every computer you crack and every puzzle you peice together is a completely new experience. 

Heck, while you're at it, go head and buy Labyrinths. It's literally a whole new game. With a whole new story line and new missions and computers and things to hack. Seriously. Do it.

And you know what? When you're done with all that, check out the Workshop! The modding community (We call ourselves Hacknet Extensions) are always pushing out new and fantastic stories and gameplay. If you really want to, you can join the Discord server and we can help you make your own (or just muck around and chat cuz we're nice people and sometimes coding gets tiring)

And hell, if you made it this far in this super long review, you might as well buy the game. It's worth it. I promise.

review_text_raw:
I’ve got Hacknet as a gift when I was learning UNIX commands and then bash scripting for work, what probably made me a perfect target player. It got me really hooked on the Linux system, and I found it a great introduction to coding as a whole. 

That said, it’s not a complicated game and no previous coding knowledge is required to play it. The "real" part mostly involves file manipulations and basic SSH usage, while the hacking part  is based on running non-real programs to break into chosen devices and perform said manipulations.

The whole game takes place in an artificial Linux environment that can be modified to a certain degree. It makes the title even more immersive and believable.

However, it’s worth noting that the core gameplay can become a little repetitive after a few hours, not to say "grindy". It’s definitely not for everyone, but the 2-hour refund window is more than enough to determine if it suits you.

review_text_raw:
[h1]10/10 will play again & buy the DLC when I have money[/h1]

I got a free copy of [i]Hacknet[/i] from a promotion on Humble Bundle without really knowing what the game was and only started playing it because of the Spring Cleaning Event here on Steam. I only intended to play it for a little bit and then move on to something else.  ...I finished the game in one sitting. Which took most of the night when I was supposed to be sleeping and I barely even noticed. Never before would I have said that a game based almost entirely around typing computer run commands would hold my interest, but [i]man[/i] was I completely enthralled start to finish.

Not only did I finish the game in one sitting, but I also immediately started over to complete side quests and find bonus material I had missed the first time around. I still haven't finished the last achievement and found all the cool hidden bonus stuff.

[u]Plot[/u]
You have been introduced into the world of hacking by Bit, another hacker who has sent you a series of automated messages fearing his own demise. [spoiler]Yes, he is actually dead. I was about an inch away from crying when it was finally confirmed late in the game.[/spoiler] Through the course of the game you work with a number of hacker communities working both as a freelance digital vigilante and trying to unravel what really happened to Bit. The plot was exciting and I ended up emotionally invested. [spoiler]There is only one ending to the game, but there are optional side quests that alter way in which you get there, as well as bonus content that appears to only be available after a restart.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Most of the gameplay is done by typing various commands into your "terminal" in much the same fashion as old-school computer programs. If you've worked with DOS or similar systems you will probably have a bit of a leg up with the basic mechanics of the game. Using those commands you hack through the security systems of other computers, copying and deleting files off their harddrives and skipping from their computers to others in their network. These hacking attempts are sometimes straightforward, sometimes more complicated with critical thinking and puzzle cracking abilities required. The further you progress in the game the more difficult they become with most of the later hacking attempts becoming a fast-paced, speeding heart race against time. There is one(?) hidden mini-game that differs from this format. [spoiler]You can find it by taking the "Pointclicker" contract from Entropy[/spoiler] Overall, I didn't think the game was very difficult, although there were plenty of challenges to overcome. I did require a walkthrough the get myself out of a tricky spot, but that was mostly due to impatience. Probably the most difficult thing in the whole game was typing commands fast enough, so those who aren't good typists might struggle more with this game.

[u]Graphics & Music[/u]
[i]Hacknet[/i] has a very simple GUI for the entire game, fairly old-school computer but with a futuristic vibe. If the color scheme bothers you, just pay attention to the achievements. ;) [spoiler]My favorite was the L-e version, I do believe.[/spoiler] The music was all low-key techno music which I quite enjoyed. Sometimes it got a bit repetitive, but it changed according to where you were in the questline, so as long as you didn't get stuck in one place for a long time (like I did, before giving up and finding a walkthrough) it was fine.

[u]Bugs & Performance[/u]
Performance wise, the game ran perfectly well on my potato laptop with only 3GB of RAM. Since the game is done almost exclusively with the keyboard, having a real one is a must IMHO, but a mouse isn't necessary. I did just fine with a trackpad. The only "bug" I encountered when playing the game is that the game crashed whenever you tabbed out of it in fullscreen mode, even if you were chilling on the main menu. So make sure you save the game before attempting to open a different window!

This game is hard to rate,

Actually i would have given a thumbs down because there are many bugs and the game is really repetitive.
You do the same commands over and over again to break into computer and it seemed kinda senseless to continue, because you dont have to think about anything if you get to know your way around. The first hour playing REALLY nice, but then you know your stuff but the game doesnt seem to evolve.

I played 6 hours in the first playthrough, but the actual playtime would have been roughly around 4 hours, if i wouldnt have been distracted. Thats not exactly much for 10 bucks (especially if its repetitive)

Furthermore the interface kinda lagged for me, which was kinda annoying.

However 2 missions (Junebug and final mission) saved it for me and i m glad i did stick around long enough.
I would like to see more missions like them!

These two missions, and the already active modding community to enhance the game, are the reasons for the thumbs up.

review_text_raw:
First of all, I never played Uplink, so I can't compare this to that. What I did play was the HackRUN saga, so please pardon my comparison to a not very similar game. I also think it's funny that there are .dll and .exe file on what is (seemingly) a Linux system, but I can ignore that.

In a nutshell, Hacknet is a hacking sim game with a decent storyline. That is something I don't see often. HackRUN also has a storyline, but it's pretty linear if you ask me. This game uses real UNIX commands. For those of you new to the coding world (I guess?), it won't be hard to pick up; the tutorial does a good job of introducing the commands, and the 'help' menu will always be there to help you. For those of you who are familiar with the UNIX command prompt, you will be pleasantly surprised. The animations you get when hacking is pretty cool too. The best part of this games\ is that there are some systems that will start tracing you once you start your hacks. You have 100 seconds to do whatever you need to do and GTFO the system, or else (I don't actually know what happens because I have never failed doing so). You can, disconnect midway to cut the trace short and come back in the system again to do your stuff (again) at a later time, but hey, where's the fun in that? Along the way of making yourself a name in the hacking world (in the game), you will encounter files that are seemingly unimportant (like IRC log files, random text files, etc.). You are half right, [b]most[/b] of these files are unimportant. They may contain jokes and the stupidity of internet friends chatting together; but the rest may contain passwords that will make your life much easier when attempting to access some systems or useful information on your target's location.

There are decent puzzles in this game that happens in a specific scenario, but the contracts you get are pretty repetitive: [spoiler]probe the system, bypass proxy/firewall if those are there, open some ports, hack in, do your stuff, clear logs, get out[/spoiler]. New commands are introduced every now and then, but those have instructions along with them, so it's pretty easy to do whatever you need to do after. Basically, it's not very challenging (unless the devs add a "No x-server" mode to force you to use the command prompt throughout the game, that would be really fun, devs pls read). The last thing that this game lacks is the ability to adjust the SFX volume. Me clicking things actually shocks me sometimes because trust me, the SFXs are loud.

In conclusion, Hacknet is a good hacking sim with a decent storyline and a bit of realism. Would I recommend? Yes. Would I play again? Yes.

If you reach this point, thank you for raking your time to read the massive wall of text that my review is (lol).

review_text_raw:
*Got the game for $2.99 during a sale*

Hacknet is an interesting game. Let's just get that out of the way. Its got a very good storyline and, while I have some experience in [strike]hacking[/strike] computer security, I didn't find (most) of the puzzles too difficult for the average person to solve. It sets a very good pace, picking up the difficulty very well. I'm writing this review just after completing the game, which took me just over 6 hours.

You start off with a message from Bit, telling you how to use the Hacknet software, etc. etc. Basically a tutorial on how to use it, the command line, that sort of thing. (If you're a linux user, this game will be much easier, the commands are basically the same for navigating the terminal and the like) After this, you're sent off to a hacker group, Entropy. You do a few hacks, and things start to pick up. You rise to the top (naturally) and start going off, investigating. I'd say more but I don't want to risk spoilers. The ending was very intriguing, and worth the effort.

The challenges are similar, but I never got bored of them. Find server at X IP, break down any proxies, firewalls, and open ports to use the almighty PortHack and get the admin password. Then, do whatever you need to, be it uploading or downloading a file, deleting stuff, or (later) even messing with databases and some... other devices. ([spoiler]a pacemaker[/spoiler]) They become more difficult as you progress, adding tracers that initiate an IP change failsafe if you take too long, more ports to open, and more complex firewalls and proxies. You'll need to grab passwords from emails and circumvent servers with powerful tracers, and even more interesting events. The only randomly difficult challenge that jumped me was an attack on my PC, which I was able to avoid using a [spoiler]trap shell[/spoiler]. If it gets you, there is a guide to help you out.

The interface is very intuitive and I never had any unreasonable issues with it, aside from becoming stuck when entering a password I didn't want to enter. (Which is my fault, I clicked login. What did I expect?) Later, you get the option to switch your layout, but none of them are really terrible. You have the terminal window (for commands), the display window (for showing the filesystem, passwords, databases, emails, etc.), the RAM window (watch this one, especially later when you get more RAM-hungry programs), and your NetMap (showing all the IPs you've connected to/can connect to).

The playtime was a good length. I would have liked it to be a bit longer but 6 hours is longer than AAA campaigns. God I hate AAA companies. Be innovative. Or I'll use Hacknet to take down your servers. /rant. Anyway, I'm not complaining about the length. As I said earlier, it never got repetitive, it was always interesting. There was always a sense of "oh gotta do this quickly or they're gonna catch me with that trace" that pushes you forward. Because of that speed though, don't play this game if you're not a quick typist. I have a speed of about 70 WPM (Faster now), which is well above average. I'd recommend being able to go above 40 WPM to play this effectively. 

------------------------------------------------------

Of course, what's a review without a pro/con list.

Pros:
+Good, interesting gameplay
+Active modding community (for extra levels and whatnot)
+Great value for the price (Yes, I know I got it for $2.99. But it's worth the full $9.99)
+Nice visuals (watch out, 1 looks like lowercase L. Tripped me up once)
+Easter Egg bash.org quotes
+Amazing soundtrack. Reflects the mood and urgency of the situations. 10/10 on that.

Neutrals:
+-Console window pops up behind game (Alt Tabbing is a little wierd)
+-Can't skip ending credits

Cons:
-You need to be a quick and accurate typist
-Requires some prior knowledge of terminal commands in order to be efficient (from the start)

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very interesting, non-repetitive gameplay and a good storyline. Visuals are of high quality and the soundtrack is amazing. However, to be good at this game you should be good at typing ( >40 WPM) and know how to navigate the Linux terminal, or at least pick up on it quickly. (I mean, it's just ls, cd, cat, and mv really) Also, bash.org quotes.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

I've just finished the Hacknet: Labyrinths DLC. I'm adding a short little note here about that.

Definetely worth it. Took an extra 3 and a half hours or so to complete, so pretty decent playtime. Much more interesing puzzles than the base game. You are tasked with completing the "Kaguya Trials" from the CSEC list, and join with a group of 3 other hackers. You'll take missions from a list and complete them with the help of the others. While you usually never actually interact with them other than seeing them in the IRC, it does feel like they're helping you. (I won't spoil how, but it becomes apparent in the endgame.) The challenges were a bit more difficult, but nothing that wasn't impossible. A mission towards the end just becomes a cat-and-mouse chase for a password, but while it didn't seem to guide you it wasn't that difficult to follow the clues. Overall, I'd highly rate the DLC. If you have the extra cash when buying Hacknet, I would recommend purchasing it. Do complete it after the main game though, or your NetMap will become a mess...

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very well done game and a great expansion to the original. I would definitely recommend purchasing this alongside the base game. Just... Play it after you beat the base game.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is an okay game, but it gets repetitive quickly. If you're unable 
to suspend your disbelief, this game might not be for you.

That being said, Hacknet does have some redeeming qualities. The game can 
serve as a tool for learning basic Linux commands, as the game involves 
spamming common terminal commands like, ls, cd, rm and scp.

Additionally, I enjoyed the creative liberties taken in the game's 
"hacking" mechanics. For example, I liked the ability to hack a fake 
cookie clicker and achieve a top score.
The actual hacking tools feel disengaging -- "SSHCrack 22 -> wait 5 seconds for it to finish "cracking" -> Porthack -> wait for it to finish "hacking" -> youre in.

Overall, while Hacknet has some interesting elements, it ultimately feels 
like a shallow experience with limited replay value.

review_text_raw:
A very introspective look at UNIX commands and the general actions of hacking - which is basically accurate, but taking out the time required to accomplish these things (for example, you can solve port protocols within a few seconds, but IRL this might take hours).

Basically, if you want the "reality" where you are the hacker in one of these movies (you're not playing the hacker, but ARE the hacker), then this is pretty spot-on. It just removes most of the tedium of the acitivites. This is not to say that the game isn't repetitive; it is, and remains true to its roots as a simulator. By nature, most simulators run off of repetitive actions which require muscle memory and timing in order to complete.

In actual fact, this is more of a puzzle-solving game. However, combined with some funny easter eggs (IRC chats can get hilarious) and honest-to-god methodology on the principles of hacking, this actually becomes enjoyable unless you just want to shoot things in the face (in which case, this is NOT the game for you).

Anyone who wants to work in software QA should be able to play this game comfortably, figure out most of the puzzles, and genuinely enjoy the experience. If you can't, don't take QA as a career. Because this in almost any form is what you do - all day, every day. I know this from 14 years of experience at that job in everything from game development to SAS or security software.

There are a few points I wish there were more of, or more developed. As game, it's pretty linear. There are nice little things like finding additional information on a server which gives you another terminal to hack, or a phone to break into, but these are too few and far between. It could be far more sandboxy if there were a freeform mode for points, which had sets of systems and connected devices which would allow you to randonly investigate things you found on another system. In this, you'd need a points system or something to gain (money, cred, whatever) - which would be a welcome addition to the game. I think another fun mode would be to actually use the system specs for the computer it was running on for memory, etc. as well as randonly generating in-game groups to become involved with, do missions for (from forums, etc.)

I recommend this game, just due to the simulation nature being captured very well. That being said, this game won't be for everyone. Much of the game is tedium and random investigation - which is exactly what hacking is about. One of the best missions which represents this is the "Project Junebug" mission. You're basically let loose to figure out how to accomlish the task, you have a lot of reading to do to catch up on how to accomplish it, and there isn't any handholding. YOU have to do the tasks, to the best of your understanding, and figure out indeed, what those tasks are, and it involves multiple servers, and different methods of having the same outcome.

Fantastic game. Beat it a while ago, but I figured I'd write a review anyway

Graphics are on point. It was very easy to get used to the interface, but I remember being a bit overwhelmed at the start. The semi-tutorial takes you through the process of the gameplay very nicely, so it's an overall smooth start.

The gameplay is fantastic. It does get a bit stale at one point in the game, and it gets a bit cryptic in some task descriptions, so I admit to having to look up a walkthrough every now and then. The puzzles are quite a lot of fun, and don't feel very repetitive, even if you get used to the generally pretty generic rhythm of the game.

There's a bit of missing suspense and a lack of clear enemies makes it a bit difficult to feel pressure when playing the game, but every now and then, a timer comes up, and it gets very dramatic, which elevates the gameplay a bit.

I loved playing it despite the small flaws. The gameplay is suprisingly riveting despite what might seem like a very simplistic set of controls. There are also tons of easter eggs hidden in the files you hack into, and reading them kinda relieves the seriousness of the game a bit, and makes room for some comedic moments

Well, I should probably say that I didn't necessarily expect one of my new favorite games of all time to be an overglorified super-hacker OS simulator, but here I am now, I guess. 

There's so much detail put into this game and it ends up becoming extremely challenging. There's a lot of learning to do in terms of what programs you need to utilize in different situations and generally how to use the interface (especially if you're not too amazingly tech-savvy). I, myself, don't consider myself anywhere near a technological expert, but I was still very easily able to get the hang of it largely due to the intricate way the game was structured and paced. There were so many things that were beautiful about this game, and I admittedly got addicted to this game. It'll probably be a game that I'll often pick back up and play over and over again in the future, and I certainly don't have any complaints in that regard. 

It may be off limits to people who are easily confused or who tend to give up on things quickly once they become overwhelmed with new information, but otherwise, this game is easily worth over $40. It's $10. Just get it.

So I just finished the game.To be honest, I'm not what to think.
First of all, I quite impressed with the amount of detail that was put into it.
On the other hand, it has a lot of missed opportunities when it come to writing, UI-Design and some mechanics.
The (mostly) reallistic terminal commands really help the [b]immersion[/b].

And that's in my opinion the main selling point of this game. 
When sitting in a dark room; late at night; typing as fast as I could to avoid being traced;
That really had me at the edge of my seat...  So recommend everyone remotely interested in
real life hacking to give it a look. It's well worth your attention.

Although, I'm not quite sure if it was worth all the time I put into it. ([spoiler]-Clock.exe-[/spoiler])

Mostly, because the different .exe exploits/scripts/hacks don't differ mechanically. It's just type whichever you see fit and wait for it to finish. Which is in my opinion the games biggest flaw. (I'm not sure I'm missing the point because it's supposed to reallistic, but after all, this is a game.)

Which is truly a shame, because these last few missions are really fun.
So if you can keep up the grind, go get and finish this.

Oh, and, I really wish to see a "Hacknet 2".

First off before I get started on this review, I want it to be kept in mind that this isn't what would be called a conventional review. So if you just want to know my answer: [/b Yes, I recommend this game. It's a super enjoyable indie game if you like the concept or idea hacking.]

Now, why this review isn't conventional comes down to this review: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/SirPenguin/recommended/365450/] [/url]
First off, it's an amazing review. However I would like to argue the points he made.

[b][i]this is a casual game[/i][/b]

This game is not intended for those that want to learn programming, it's not intended for those that want to write lines of code out and debug and test it...while yes that is more realistic, what would you rather do, play a casual game and be immersed in the story and puzzles, or have to write out lines of code in order to solve the issues in front of you? (Probably spending tedious hours being bored trying to debug your code)

You'd probably prefer to use the commands the game has pre-made for you. The game design was intentional, most people wouldn't want something that get's "taken to the next level"...at least to the point of writing out lines of code by hand. In fact, most people probably won't have coding experience.

The game is a Story rich simulation game. Not a code markup tool. Not a learning game. It's made to be a fun unique puzzle game. So while regardless you'll probably find enjoyment out of the game, don't go into it expecting to find some crazy challenging puzzle that requires you to write out lines of code by hand, developing your own "hacking tools". Expect a fast pace story rich hacking game.

While I respect the points made in the above review, I felt it necessary to explain what you are really going to get out of this game, instead of a false idea of what it really is.

In fact, most people probably won't have coding experience. The game is a Story rich simulation game. Not a code markup tool. Not a learning game. It's made to be a fun unique puzzle game. So while regardless you'll probably find enjoyment out of the game, don't go into it expecting to find some crazy challenging puzzle that requires you to write out lines of code by hand, developing your own "hacking tools". Expect a fast pace story rich hacking game. While I respect the points made in the above review, I felt it necessary to explain what you are really going to get out of this game, instead of a false idea of what it really is.

review_text_raw:
[h1][b]IF YOU LIKE THE IDEA OF A GAME FOCUSING ENTIRELY ON A TERMINAL/COMMAND-LINE AND SOME EASY TO MODERATELY DIFFICULT PUZZLES THROWN IN, YOU MAY LIKE THIS GAME.[/b][/h1]
As someone who has a bit of experience with the UNIX terminal and commands, this game had my absolute full attention and felt familiar to me. [b]I've just recently bought this game (yesterday, at the time of writing) and I was absolutely HOOKED and couldn't get away from it. Hacknet is absolutely my style of game! (right now, I've just beaten the base game and will go through the DLC content shortly. but I may fiddle around with the Extensions)[/b]

[h1][b]TARGET[/b][/h1]
Obviously, this game isn't for everyone. A terminal-based game can seem intimidating or uninteresting to someone who has no experience with it before (and even if you do, a terminal-based game may not be that interesting). If the screenshots and description provided by the game do not capture your attention, it's probably not the game for you. But if your curiosity is piqued, it may be a great experience for you.

[h1][b]PUZZLE ELEMENTS AND TUTORIALS[/b][/h1]
Hacknet introduces itself quite well to the uninformed, and doesn't hand-hold. It throws you straight in after a short tutorial on using the terminal and interface, therefore encouraging experimentation with what you have available. By not holding the player's hand, succeeding in the puzzles without any additional help besides what the game provides will give you a sense of accomplishment. However, that can turn some people off, and if it does, it may not be for you.

It is possible to get stuck in several points in the game, but no solution is too far out there and is solvable without a walkthrough. (and I admit, I have, and have consulted a walkthrough but I was extra careful not to look any further ahead than the current task at hand, most of the time I had just forgotten something simple and was able to get back on track quickly).

The puzzles start off pretty easy, leading you on and increasing the difficulty as it goes, pretty much gently guiding you on how to work with the game's unique nature.

At certain times, the tasks can seem repetitive, and to be fair, it is. You are constantly trying to break into a lot of different computers, servers, devices, etc. but that's what it is. It is an accurate representation instead of the flashy Hollywood style hacking seen on film (but it certainly can be flashy when it wants to be and is for certain parts).

[h1][b]STORY[/b][/h1]
The story itself is nothing outstanding, but it certainly fits the theme and style of the game. It's perfect for the game. The story is there for the beginning and the end of your gameplay, giving you purpose to start and an objective to reach near the end. In the middle of the game, you are given freedom to do what you wish. Or PointClicker, if that's your thing (I won't judge!).

[h1][b]MUSIC[/b][/h1]
The music is an absolute fit for Hacknet and I often found myself focusing on the killer beats rather than what's at hand. It also made me quite shaky during the parts that are time-based.

[h1][b]OVERALL[/b][/h1]
Overall, Hacknet is extremely accurate compared to other things that have tried to display this kind of topic before. The elements work wonderfully and the balance between gameplay and the real elements is on point (all the commands given are used at one point or another and no unnecessary garbage is there). To the average person who may not know anything about the terminal, it can be exciting to get into it for the first time not knowing anything and eventually learn (there may be a little higher risk of getting stuck at a point, but that's okay!). To those who are a little familiar with the terminal and commands, you'll feel right at home and understand the game quickly and have a great time with it!

[h1][b]SHOULD YOU GET IT?[/b][/h1]
If this game looks interesting, [b]IT WILL BE FOR YOU.[/b] The terminal looks intimidating from the start, and if that doesn't deter you and the description of the game brings you in further, you [b]WILL[/b] enjoy it!
